label: Rigid-Body Motions
notes: This central chapter spans printed pages 59 through 136 and builds the geometric language of robotics. We represent a displacement, a velocity, and a force without losing frame information, moving from the rotation group through homogeneous transforms, twists, screws, and wrenches toward a single coherent picture of rigid motion.

label: Rotation Matrices and SO(3)
notes: A rotation matrix stores an orthonormal right-handed frame in its columns. The constraints of orthogonality and unit determinant cut the nine entries down to three degrees of freedom, defining the special orthogonal group SO(3), a curved manifold rather than a flat vector space of matrices.

label: Angular Velocity and so(3)
notes: Differentiating the orthogonality constraint shows that the velocity of a rotation is a skew-symmetric matrix times the rotation. Skew-symmetric matrices form the Lie algebra so(3), the tangent space at the identity, and the bracket notation packages an angular velocity vector into that matrix.

label: Exponential Coordinates of Rotation
notes: Rotating about a unit axis omega by angle theta is the matrix exponential of the skew matrix scaled by theta. This exponential map sends the flat Lie algebra onto the curved group, so axis and angle become a chart of three exponential coordinates for any rotation.

label: Rodrigues' Formula
notes: The matrix exponential closes into a finite formula because powers of a unit skew matrix cycle. Rodrigues' formula expresses the rotation using sine and cosine of the angle, giving a cheap, numerically stable way to convert axis-angle coordinates into a concrete rotation matrix without an infinite series.

label: Matrix Logarithm of Rotation
notes: The inverse problem recovers an axis and angle from a rotation matrix using the matrix logarithm. The trace fixes the angle and the antisymmetric part fixes the axis, but the chart degenerates near angle pi and at the identity, exactly where careful implementations must branch.

label: Homogeneous Transforms and SE(3)
notes: Stacking a rotation block and a translation into a four-by-four matrix represents a full rigid displacement. These homogeneous transforms form the special Euclidean group SE(3); composing motions becomes matrix multiplication, and the inverse is built cheaply from the transpose of the rotation block.

label: Twists and Spatial Velocity
notes: The velocity of a rigid body packs an angular part and a linear part into a six-vector twist, the tangent object of SE(3). Its matrix form lives in the Lie algebra se(3), and choosing the space frame or the body frame changes which twist we read.

label: Screw Motion: Chasles-Mozzi
notes: The Chasles-Mozzi theorem states that every rigid displacement is a screw: a rotation about an axis combined with a translation along that same axis. The pitch h measures translation per radian, unifying pure rotations, pure translations, and the general helical motion into one geometric primitive.

label: Exponential Coordinates of SE(3)
notes: A finite rigid motion is the matrix exponential of a twist times the displacement angle, generalizing Rodrigues' formula to se(3). The six exponential coordinates are a screw axis scaled by distance traveled, and the matrix logarithm recovers that screw from any homogeneous transform.

label: Wrenches: Force and Moment
notes: A wrench pairs a moment and a force into a six-vector dual to the twist. The instantaneous power is their inner product, a frame-independent scalar. Because power must be invariant, wrenches transform by the dual rule, marking them as covectors rather than ordinary vectors.

label: The Adjoint Representation
notes: The adjoint map built from a transform changes the frame in which a twist is expressed while preserving the physical motion. Its inverse transpose carries wrenches the dual way, so the power pairing between a twist and a wrench stays constant across any change of frame.

label: Synthesis and Sanity Checks
notes: Rigid motion lives on Lie groups, and twists and wrenches are dual partners joined by power. The notebook confirms the picture numerically: exponential and logarithm round trips vanish, rigid maps preserve distances, and the adjoint keeps twist and wrench power pairings invariant to machine precision.
